paragraphs.text: וַֽיְהִ֥י כָל־הָאָ֖רֶץ שָׂפָ֣ה אֶחָ֑ת וּדְבָרִ֖ים אֲחָדִֽים׃

i18n.en: The whole land was of one lip and one set of words.
i18n.he: וַֽיְהִ֥י כָל־הָאָ֖רֶץ שָׂפָ֣ה אֶחָ֑ת וּדְבָרִ֖ים אֲחָדִֽים׃
i18n.de: Das ganze Land hatte eine Lippe und einerlei Worte.
i18n.es: Toda la tierra era de un solo labio y unas mismas palabras.
i18n.fr: Toute la terre avait une seule langue et un seul vocabulaire.
i18n.ja: 全地は一つの言葉、一つの語彙であった。
i18n.ko: 온 땅이 하나의 입술, 하나의 말의 모음이었다.
i18n.ru: И была вся земля одного языка и одних слов.
i18n.zh: 全地都是同一种语言、同一套话语。
i18n.zh-Hant: 全地都是同一種語言、一樣的話語。

notes.official:
**The opening claim is doubled.** *Safa achat* — *one lip* — and *devarim achadim* — *one set of words*. The two phrases name distinct dimensions of linguistic unity. *Safa* — שָׂפָה — is literally the speech-organ ('lip'); the metonymy for *language* is well-attested in Hebrew (cf. Isa 19:18 'the lip of Canaan' = the Canaanite language). *Devarim* — דְּבָרִים — is *words / matters / things*. The doubled claim is: the whole land had not only a shared phonology and grammar (one *lip*) but a shared semantic stock (one set of *words / matters*).

The verse stands in tension with 10:5, 10:20, 10:31, which described the Japhethites, Hamites, and Shemites as already differentiated by *tongues* (*lashon*). The chapter is opening a parallel timeline — or the redactor has preserved two distinct traditions about linguistic origins, with the Table of Nations chapter and the Babel chapter belonging to different source-strands. The standard scholarly attribution: chapter 10 is the Priestly (P) ethnography; chapter 11:1–9 is the Yahwist (J) etiology. The redactor placed them side-by-side and left the seam visible.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְהִ֖י בְּנָסְעָ֣ם מִקֶּ֑דֶם וַֽיִּמְצְא֥וּ בִקְעָ֛ה בְּאֶ֥רֶץ שִׁנְעָ֖ר וַיֵּ֥שְׁבוּ שָֽׁם׃

i18n.en: As they journeyed from the east, they found a valley in the land of Shinar, and they settled there.
i18n.he: וַֽיְהִ֖י בְּנָסְעָ֣ם מִקֶּ֑דֶם וַֽיִּמְצְא֥וּ בִקְעָ֛ה בְּאֶ֥רֶץ שִׁנְעָ֖ר וַיֵּ֥שְׁבוּ שָֽׁם׃
i18n.de: Und es geschah, als sie von Osten aufbrachen, da fanden sie eine Talebene im Land Schinar und ließen sich dort nieder.
i18n.es: Y aconteció que, al partir del oriente, hallaron un valle en la tierra de Sinar, y se establecieron allí.
i18n.fr: Comme ils partaient de l'orient, ils trouvèrent une vallée au pays de Shinéar, et ils s'y établirent.
i18n.ja: 人々は東から旅をしてきて、シナルの地に谷を見いだし、そこに住みついた。
i18n.ko: 그들이 동쪽에서 이동하다가, 시날 땅에서 한 골짜기를 발견하고 거기에 정착하였다.
i18n.ru: И было, как двинулись они с востока, нашли они долину в земле Шинар и поселились там.
i18n.zh: 他们从东方迁移的时候，在示拿地遇见一片平原，就在那里定居下来。
i18n.zh-Hant: 他們從東方遷移時，在示拿地遇見一片平原，就住在那裡。

notes.official:
**Eastward, or from the east?** מִקֶּדֶם *miqedem* has the same ambiguity here as in 2:8 (where the garden was planted *miqedem*): it can mean *from the east* (the people are coming westward from a more easterly origin) or *eastward* (they are journeying in an eastward direction). The standard reading is *from the east* — the post-Flood humans, descending from Noah's ark on the mountains of Ararat (8:4) in the Armenian highlands, are migrating south and west into the Mesopotamian alluvium.

*Biqah b'eretz Shinar* — *a valley in the land of Shinar*. The same Shinar named in 10:10 (the location of Nimrod's Babel, Erech, Akkad, Calneh). The chapter is geographically continuous with chapter 10's Nimrod parenthesis: the same southern-Mesopotamian alluvial plain, the same proto-civilization context. *Biqah* — *valley, plain* — names the flat alluvium itself; the contrast with Levantine hill-country is implicit.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּאמְר֞וּ אִ֣ישׁ אֶל־רֵעֵ֗הוּ הָ֚בָה נִלְבְּנָ֣ה לְבֵנִ֔ים וְנִשְׂרְפָ֖ה לִשְׂרֵפָ֑ה וַתְּהִ֨י לָהֶ֤ם הַלְּבֵנָה֙ לְאָ֔בֶן וְהַ֣חֵמָ֔ר הָיָ֥ה לָהֶ֖ם לַחֹֽמֶר׃

i18n.en: They said each to his neighbor, "Come, let us make bricks, and burn them in fire." The brick was for them as stone, and the bitumen was for them as mortar.
i18n.he: וַיֹּאמְר֞וּ אִ֣ישׁ אֶל־רֵעֵ֗הוּ הָ֚בָה נִלְבְּנָ֣ה לְבֵנִ֔ים וְנִשְׂרְפָ֖ה לִשְׂרֵפָ֑ה וַתְּהִ֨י לָהֶ֤ם הַלְּבֵנָה֙ לְאָ֔בֶן וְהַ֣חֵמָ֔ר הָיָ֥ה לָהֶ֖ם לַחֹֽמֶר׃
i18n.de: Und sie sprachen einer zum andern: "Wohlan, laßt uns Ziegel streichen und sie im Feuer brennen." Und der Ziegel diente ihnen als Stein, und das Erdharz diente ihnen als Mörtel.
i18n.es: Y se dijeron uno a otro: «Vamos, hagamos ladrillos, y cozámoslos en el fuego». Y el ladrillo les sirvió por piedra, y el asfalto por mortero.
i18n.fr: Ils se dirent l'un à l'autre : « Allons, faisons des briques et cuisons-les au feu. » La brique leur servit de pierre, et le bitume leur servit de mortier.
i18n.ja: 彼らは互いに言った、「さあ、れんがを作って、火で焼こう」。そして彼らにとって、石の代わりにれんががあり、モルタルの代わりにアスファルトがあった。
i18n.ko: 그들이 서로 이웃에게 말하였다, "오라, 벽돌을 만들어 불에 구워 보자." 그들에게는 벽돌이 돌 대신이었고, 역청이 회 대신이었다.
i18n.ru: И сказали друг другу: «Давайте наделаем кирпичей и обожжём огнём». И были у них кирпичи вместо камня, а смола вместо извести.
i18n.zh: 他们彼此说：「来吧，我们做砖，用火烧透。」于是砖对他们如同石头，沥青对他们如同砂浆。
i18n.zh-Hant: 他們彼此說：「來吧，我們作磚把火燒透。」他們就用磚代替石頭，又用瀝青代替砂漿。

notes.official:
**The first human cohortative.** *Havah nilbenah* — *come, let us make bricks*. *Havah* (an interjection, 'come!') plus the first-person plural cohortative *nilbenah*. The verb is built on the same noun *l'venah* (brick); the wordplay is *nilbenah l'venim* — *let us brick bricks*. The doubled construction repeats in the next clause: *nisrefah lisrefah* — *let us burn (them) with a burning*.

The chapter is opening on a HUMAN cohortative — *let us...* — that will be echoed structurally three times: here (v3), in the city-and-tower decision (v4 *havah nivneh*), and then mirrored from the divine side (v7 *havah neredah*). The cohortative becomes the chapter's rhetorical signature, and the chapter ends by showing the divine cohortative answering the human ones.

*Ha-l'venah l'aven v'ha-chemar laya lahem la-chomer* — *the brick was for them as stone, and the bitumen as mortar*. The aside is technological-archaeological: it notes that the southern Mesopotamian builders, lacking stone (the alluvium has none), substituted kiln-fired clay brick with bitumen mortar. This is empirically accurate to the construction methods of southern Mesopotamian ziggurats, attested archaeologically and in Mesopotamian texts. The chapter is technically literate about the construction methods of the world it describes.

i18n.he: וַיֹּאמְר֞וּ הָ֣בָה ׀ נִבְנֶה־לָּ֣נוּ עִ֗יר וּמִגְדָּל֙ וְרֹאשׁ֣וֹ בַשָּׁמַ֔יִם וְנַֽעֲשֶׂה־לָּ֖נוּ שֵׁ֑ם פֶּן־נָפ֖וּץ עַל־פְּנֵ֥י כָל־הָאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.es: Dijeron: «Vamos, edifiquémonos una ciudad y una torre cuya cúspide llegue a los cielos; y hagámonos un nombre, no sea que seamos dispersados sobre la faz de toda la tierra».
i18n.fr: Ils dirent : « Allons, bâtissons-nous une ville, et une tour dont le sommet soit dans les cieux ; et faisons-nous un nom, de peur que nous ne soyons dispersés sur la face de toute la terre. »

i18n.ko: 그들이 말하였다, "오라, 우리 자신을 위하여 성읍을 짓고, 그 꼭대기가 하늘에 닿는 탑을 짓자; 우리 자신을 위하여 이름을 떨치자, 우리가 온 땅의 표면 위에 흩어지지 않도록."

i18n.zh: 他们说：「来吧，我们为自己建一座城和一座塔，塔顶通天；我们要为自己立名，免得我们被分散在全地之面上。」
i18n.zh-Hant: 他們說：「來吧，我們要為自己建造一座城和一座塔，塔頂通到諸天；讓我們為自己揚名，免得我們被分散在全地的表面。」

notes.official:
**The chapter's keystone verse — three intentions stated in one breath.**

First, *havah nivneh lanu ir umigdal* — *come, let us build for ourselves a city and a tower*. The pair *ir* (city) and *migdal* (tower) names the political-architectural project. *Migdal* is the ziggurat — the stepped temple-platform of Mesopotamian religious architecture, exemplified by the great ziggurat of Etemenanki at Babylon (the Esagila complex), the most famous of which was rebuilt by Nebuchadnezzar II in the 6th c. BCE. The chapter is reading the ziggurat-tradition, not inventing it.

Second, *v'rosho bashamayim* — *with its top in the skies*. *Rosho* (its head/top) reaching *bashamayim* (in the skies). The phrase is not necessarily a literal claim that the tower will physically reach the heavens; *rosho bashamayim* is a stock-phrase for *very tall* (cf. Deut 1:28, 9:1, of fortified cities 'whose walls reach up to the skies'). But in this chapter the phrase carries more than hyperbole: the ziggurat's *function* was to be a stairway between earth and the divine realm — the Mesopotamian theology of the ziggurat is that the deity descended onto the platform-shrine at its summit, and that human worship ascended through it. *Rosho bashamayim* is naming the ziggurat's *aspiration*, not just its dimension.

Third, *v'na'aseh lanu shem* — *and let us make for ourselves a name*. This is the chapter's most lens-charged phrase. The cohortative *naase* — *let us make* — is the same form as Genesis 1:26's *naase adam* — *let us make humankind*. There it was the Elohim speaking; here it is humans. The chapter is staging humans assuming the divine cohortative register — the *naase adam* of creation is mirrored by the *naase lanu shem* of the post-Flood project. The verbal parallel is exact, and the chapter is silent about whether to read this as imitation, presumption, or aspiration.

*Shem* — *name* — in Hebrew Bible idiom is not just an identifying label but renown, reputation, lasting memory (cf. 2 Sam 7:9, of YHWH making David's *shem* great). The phrase *anshei ha-shem* — *men of name* — was applied in 6:4 to the antediluvian *gibborim*; now in 11:4 the post-Flood humans propose to *make for themselves a name*. The chapter is connecting the human ambition at Babel to the *gibborim*-class register the Flood was supposed to have ended.

*Pen-naputz al-pnei kol ha-aretz* — *lest we be scattered upon the face of the whole land*. The motive is given as fear of dispersion. The verb *putz* (to scatter, disperse) will return in v8 (*vayyafetz YHWH otam*) — what they feared is what happens, brought about by the very God they were trying to overshoot.

paragraphs.text: וַיֵּ֣רֶד יְהוָ֔ה לִרְאֹ֥ת אֶת־הָעִ֖יר וְאֶת־הַמִּגְדָּ֑ל אֲשֶׁ֥ר בָּנ֖וּ בְּנֵ֥י הָאָדָֽם׃

i18n.he: וַיֵּ֣רֶד יְהוָ֔ה לִרְאֹ֥ת אֶת־הָעִ֖יר וְאֶת־הַמִּגְדָּ֑ל אֲשֶׁ֥ר בָּנ֖וּ בְּנֵ֥י הָאָדָֽם׃
i18n.de: Da stieg YHWH herab, um die Stadt und den Turm zu sehen, die die Söhne des Menschen gebaut hatten.
i18n.es: Y YHWH descendió para ver la ciudad y la torre que habían edificado los hijos del ser humano.
i18n.fr: YHWH descendit pour voir la ville et la tour que les fils des hommes avaient bâties.
i18n.ja: YHWHは、人の息子たちが建てた町と塔とを見るために降りてこられた。
i18n.ko: YHWH가 사람의 아들들이 지은 성읍과 탑을 보러 내려오셨다.
i18n.ru: И сошёл YHWH посмотреть город и башню, которые строили сыны человеческие.
i18n.zh: YHWH 降临，要看人之子们所建造的城和塔。
i18n.zh-Hant: YHWH 降臨，要看看人的兒子們所建造的城和塔。

notes.official:
***Vayered YHWH*** — *YHWH came down*. The verb is יָרַד *yarad* — *descend* — used here with YHWH as subject. The anthropomorphic register is plain: YHWH is positioned *above*, the city-and-tower is *below*, and YHWH *descends* to see it. The descent is the inverse of the tower's ascent: the humans build *upward* (with its top in the skies); YHWH comes *down* to inspect. The verbal pairing is the chapter's structural irony — the tower designed to reach the divine realm prompts the divine being to descend, with results the humans did not intend.

The descent-language will recur in v7 (*havah neredah* — *let us go down*) when YHWH speaks in the divine cohortative. The chapter has two descents: v5 (singular YHWH *yarad* — sees) and v7 (plural *neredah* — acts).

*Bnei ha-adam* — *the sons of the human / sons of humankind*. The phrase emphasizes the lineage: these are descendants of the *adam* of Genesis 2–3. The chapter is connecting Babel-builders to the Edenic origin — they are doing what humans do, building what humans build, asserting what humans assert.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יְהוָ֗ה הֵ֣ן עַ֤ם אֶחָד֙ וְשָׂפָ֤ה אַחַת֙ לְכֻלָּ֔ם וְזֶ֖ה הַחִלָּ֣ם לַעֲשׂ֑וֹת וְעַתָּה֙ לֹֽא־יִבָּצֵ֣ר מֵהֶ֔ם כֹּ֛ל אֲשֶׁ֥ר יָזְמ֖וּ לַֽעֲשֽׂוֹת׃

notes.official:
**The chapter's load-bearing claim.** YHWH's assessment has three components.

First, *am echad v'safa achat l'kulam* — *one people and one tongue for all of them*. The unity is named twice — *one people, one tongue*. The verse is acknowledging that unified human coordination is what enables what follows.

Second, *zeh hachilam la'asot* — *this is what they begin to do*. The verb הֵחֵל *hechel* — *began* — is the same verb that opened the Nimrod parenthesis (*hu hechel lihyot gibbor*, 10:8). The chapter is reading the Babel project as the *beginning* of unified human technological-political ambition, not the end of it.

Third, the keystone clause: *v'atah lo yibatzer mehem kol asher yazmu la'asot* — *and now, nothing will be withheld from them which they have schemed to do*. The verb בָּצַר *batsar* — *to restrain, hold back, make inaccessible* — appears in the passive niphal (*yibatzer*): nothing will *be made inaccessible* to them. The clause is YHWH's plain claim that human coordination at this scale produces unlimited capacity. The verb *yazmu* (from *zamam*, 'devise, scheme, plan') is neutral-to-negative in its semantic range — it covers planning generally but is often used of *premeditation* in legal contexts.

The Wheel of Heaven reading hears this verse with unusual clarity. The divine assessment is *not* that what the humans are doing is metaphysically wrong (no curse-language is used, no judicial register); it is that what they are doing is *technologically open-ended*. The response in v7 will be a deliberate intervention to break the coordination — not a punishment but a *cap on capacity*. The chapter is staging a strategic divine response to human power-aggregation. The lens reads this against the canon's framing of the Elohim as a senior civilization that has reasons to manage human technological progress.

notes.official:
**The third explicit divine cohortative in Genesis.** *Havah neredah v'navlah* — *come, let us go down, and let us confuse*.

The first was 1:26 — *naase adam b'tsalmenu kidmutenu* (*let us make humankind in our image, in our likeness*) — at the creation of humankind. The second was 3:22 — *hen ha-adam haya k'achad mimennu lada'at tov vara* (*behold, the human has become like one of us, knowing good and bad*) — after the Tree-eating. The third is 11:7. All three are first-person *plural* speech with divine subject.

The pattern across the three: at 1:26 the divine plural *makes* humankind; at 3:22 the divine plural recognizes that humankind has become *like* the divine plural in a specific capacity; at 11:7 the divine plural intervenes to *cap* what humankind can do together. The Genesis primaeval-history arc, on the chapter's textual surface, is the story of a divine-plural class managing the emergence of a human-collective whose capacity is approaching theirs. The chapter does not editorialize on this reading; it preserves the grammatical plural and lets the reader draw the structural pattern.

The cohortative *havah neredah* — *come, let us go down* — is the mirror of the humans' *havah nilbenah* (v3) and *havah nivneh* (v4). The chapter has stacked four cohortatives in nine verses: two human (let us brick / let us build), two divine (let us go down / let us confuse). The verbal symmetry is the chapter's most precise structural feature. The humans' cohortative-projects produce a divine cohortative-response. The chapter is composed with a careful sense of rhetorical match.

*V'navlah sham sefatam* — *let us confuse their tongue there*. The verb בָּלַל *balal* — *mix, confound, confuse* — is the etymological root of *Babel* (v9). The intervention is *linguistic*: not destroying the city, not killing the builders, but breaking the *coordination capability* by fragmenting the shared language. The response is targeted: it removes the specific affordance that made the project possible.

notes.official:
**Their fear is fulfilled by the divine action.** The humans had said in v4: *pen-naputz al-pnei kol ha-aretz* — *lest we be scattered upon the face of the whole land*. The verse now reports: *vayyafetz YHWH otam ... al-pnei kol ha-aretz* — *YHWH scattered them ... upon the face of the whole land*. The exact phrase the humans had used in their fear-clause is now used in the action-clause, with YHWH as the subject of the verb the humans had used in the passive.

The verb is the same root (פוץ *putz*); the humans feared the dispersal that the divine action then produced. The chapter is reading the Babel project as motivated by the fear of dispersion, and the divine response as enacting exactly what the project was designed to prevent.

*Vayyachdelu livnot ha-ir* — *and they ceased to build the city*. The verb *chadal* (cease) is the gentlest possible language for project-stop: not destroyed, not punished, not killed. The construction simply *halts* when the linguistic coordination fails. The chapter is technically accurate about the social mechanism: large-scale construction projects collapse when communication breaks down. The divine intervention is engineering-grade: minimal, targeted, sufficient.

notes.official:
**The etymology and the closing summary.** *Babel* — בָּבֶל — and *balal* — בָּלַל — share a triconsonantal root structure (b-b-l / b-l-l) close enough for the chapter to assert an etymological pun. The actual etymology is contested: the Hebrew *Babel* most likely derives from the Akkadian *Bab-ilim* (*'gate of the gods'*) — the same name that gives English *Babylon*. The chapter is offering a *folk etymology* that recodes the city's name from *gate of the gods* (the Mesopotamian self-naming) into *the place of confusion* (the Hebrew Bible's reframing). The pun is theological re-naming: the Mesopotamian city of divine access is recast as the city of divine refusal of access.

The chapter closes the Babel narrative and pivots to the Shem-genealogy that will land at Abraham. The reader is to keep two things in view: (1) the divine assessment that human coordination at scale was approaching divine capacity, and (2) the divine response of fragmentation. The line that will run from v10 down to v26 — Shem to Abram — is the *new* divine project after the cap was imposed. The chapter's structural logic: humanity *en masse* could not be permitted to continue at Babel; the next chapter will start the *covenant-line* of Abraham. The two are sequential narrative moves.

notes.official:
**The toledot of Shem opens.** This is the fifth *toledot* in Genesis (after 2:4 of the skies, 5:1 of Adam, 6:9 of Noah, 10:1 of Noah's sons). The genealogy that follows is the structural counterpart to chapter 5: ten generations, each with the formula *X lived Y years, fathered Z; and X lived W years after fathering Z, and fathered sons and daughters*. The pattern is identical to chapter 5; what differs is the *length* of lives — the post-Flood lifespans drop steadily across the ten generations from ~600 (Shem) down to ~205 (Terah, v32).

*Shenatayim achar ha-mabbul* — *two years after the deluge*. The dating-by-Flood-event continues the chronological grid of chapter 5–9; it also closes the chronological loop: the Flood is the anchor-event, with all subsequent dates measured from it.

notes.official: **Eber, the eponymous Hebrew ancestor.** עֵבֶר *Eber* is the etymological source most commonly proposed for עִבְרִי *Ivri* (Hebrew), the gentilic that Abraham will be called in 14:13. The chapter places Eber in the central position of the Shem-genealogy: four generations after Shem, with Abraham coming four generations after Eber. The genealogy is structured to make Eber the symbolic midpoint between the post-Flood patriarch and the covenant-founder.

notes.official: **The lifespans drop.** Peleg's total lifespan (239 years) is less than half of his great-grandfather Shem's (600 years). The compression of post-Flood lives — already attested in chapter 5 with Adam's 930 and Methuselah's 969 — is accelerating in chapter 11. By Terah (v32, 205 years), the antediluvian-scale lifespans are gone. The chapter does not comment on the compression. The patriarchal narratives that follow (Abraham 175, Isaac 180, Jacob 147) will continue the decline.

i18n.es: Téraj vivió setenta años y engendró a Abram, Najor y Harán.
i18n.fr: Térah vécut soixante-dix ans et engendra Abram, Nahor et Harân.
i18n.ja: テラは七十年生きて、アブラム、ナホル、ハランをもうけた。
i18n.ko: 데라는 칠십 년을 살았고 아브람, 나홀, 하란을 낳았다.
i18n.ru: Терах жил семьдесят лет и родил Аврама, Нахора и Арана.
i18n.zh: 他拉活了七十岁，生了亚伯兰、拿鹤、哈兰。
i18n.zh-Hant: 他拉活了七十年，生了亞伯蘭、拿鶴、哈蘭。

notes.official:
**The decade-genealogy lands at the threshold.** The ten-generation sequence from Shem to Abram parallels the ten-generation sequence from Adam to Noah in chapter 5. The structural parallel is deliberate: each ten-generation arc anchors a turning point — Noah for the Flood, Abram for the covenant.

*Abram* enters Genesis here, the first explicit mention. The reader who has been following the toledot-arc since chapter 5 has been waiting for this moment for two chapters. The naming triad — Abram, Nachor, Haran — places Abram first by prominence (not necessarily by birth-order; *vayyoled et X et Y v'et Z* is the standard naming-by-importance pattern, as with Shem-Ham-Yepheth).

paragraphs.text: וְאֵ֙לֶּה֙ תּוֹלְדֹ֣ת תֶּ֔רַח תֶּ֚רַח הוֹלִ֣יד אֶת־אַבְרָ֔ם אֶת־נָח֖וֹר וְאֶת־הָרָ֑ן וְהָרָ֖ן הוֹלִ֥יד אֶת־לֽוֹט׃

i18n.en: These are the begettings of Terah. Terah fathered Abram, Nachor, and Haran; and Haran fathered Lot.
i18n.he: וְאֵ֙לֶּה֙ תּוֹלְדֹ֣ת תֶּ֔רַח תֶּ֚רַח הוֹלִ֣יד אֶת־אַבְרָ֔ם אֶת־נָח֖וֹר וְאֶת־הָרָ֑ן וְהָרָ֖ן הוֹלִ֥יד אֶת־לֽוֹט׃
i18n.de: Und dies ist die Folge der Zeugungen Terachs. Terach zeugte Abram, Nachor und Haran; und Haran zeugte Lot.
i18n.es: Estas son las generaciones de Téraj. Téraj engendró a Abram, Najor y Harán; y Harán engendró a Lot.
i18n.fr: Voici les générations de Térah. Térah engendra Abram, Nahor et Harân ; et Harân engendra Lot.
i18n.ja: これはテラの系図である。テラはアブラム、ナホル、ハランをもうけた。ハランはロトをもうけた。
i18n.ko: 이것은 데라의 계보이다. 데라는 아브람, 나홀, 하란을 낳았고; 하란은 롯을 낳았다.
i18n.ru: Вот родословие Тераха. Терах родил Аврама, Нахора и Арана; а Аран родил Лота.
i18n.zh: 这是他拉的世系。他拉生了亚伯兰、拿鹤、哈兰；哈兰生了罗得。
i18n.zh-Hant: 這是他拉的世系。他拉生了亞伯蘭、拿鶴、哈蘭；哈蘭生了羅得。

notes.official: **The sixth toledot in Genesis opens.** The chapter has now stacked three toledot-formulae in two chapters (10:1 Noah's sons; 11:10 Shem; 11:27 Terah), each narrowing the focus: from the post-Flood world to the Shemite line to the household of Terah. The narrowing prepares the move from cosmic-ethnographic scope to family-narrative scope that will run through chapters 12–50.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּ֣מָת הָרָ֔ן עַל־פְּנֵ֖י תֶּ֣רַח אָבִ֑יו בְּאֶ֥רֶץ מוֹלַדְתּ֖וֹ בְּא֥וּר כַּשְׂדִּֽים׃

i18n.en: Haran died in the presence of Terah his father, in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Kasdim.
i18n.he: וַיָּ֣מָת הָרָ֔ן עַל־פְּנֵ֖י תֶּ֣רַח אָבִ֑יו בְּאֶ֥רֶץ מוֹלַדְתּ֖וֹ בְּא֥וּר כַּשְׂדִּֽים׃
i18n.de: Und Haran starb im Angesicht Terachs, seines Vaters, im Land seiner Geburt, in Ur der Kasdim.
i18n.es: Y murió Harán en presencia de Téraj su padre, en la tierra de su nacimiento, en Ur de los caldeos.
i18n.fr: Harân mourut en présence de Térah son père, dans le pays de sa naissance, à Our des Chaldéens.
i18n.ja: ハランは、その父テラの目の前で、その生まれた地、カルデアのウルで死んだ。
i18n.ko: 하란은 자기가 태어난 땅, 갈대아의 우르에서, 자기 아버지 데라 앞에서 죽었다.
i18n.ru: И умер Аран при Терахе, отце своём, в земле рождения своего, в Уре Халдейском.
i18n.zh: 哈兰死在他父亲他拉面前，在他出生之地，迦勒底的吾珥。
i18n.zh-Hant: 哈蘭死在他父親他拉之前，在他出生之地—迦勒底的吾珥。

notes.official:
**The first recorded child-predeceasing-parent in Genesis.** *Vayyamat Haran al-pnei Terah aviv* — *Haran died in the presence of Terah his father*. The phrase *al-pnei* (literally 'upon the face of') in the context of death means *during the lifetime of* — Haran predeceased his father, the reverse of the patriarchal-norm in which the father dies first. The narrative aside marks the death as out-of-order.

*Ur Kasdim* — *Ur of the Kasdim*. Ur was the great Sumerian city of southern Mesopotamia, capital of the Third Dynasty of Ur (ca. 2100 BCE), excavated by Leonard Woolley in the 1920s. The qualifier *Kasdim* (Chaldeans) is anachronistic: the Chaldeans are a first-millennium-BCE Aramean people who came to dominate Babylonia in the Neo-Babylonian period. *Ur Kasdim* is therefore a chronologically-confused identifier — the city of Ur but with its later-conquering people's name attached. Modern scholarly debate has proposed alternative identifications (a northern Mesopotamian *Ur* near Haran, rather than the famous southern *Ur*) precisely to avoid the *Kasdim* anachronism. The chapter is naming the family's place of origin in Mesopotamia, with vocabulary that mixes geographic eras. The Wheel of Heaven lens reads Abram's family as Mesopotamian in origin — the same alluvial plain that hosted Nimrod's Babel — preparing the reader for chapter 12's move out of that civilization.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקַּ֨ח אַבְרָ֧ם וְנָח֛וֹר לָהֶ֖ם נָשִׁ֑ים שֵׁ֤ם אֵֽשֶׁת־אַבְרָם֙ שָׂרָ֔י וְשֵׁ֤ם אֵֽשֶׁת־נָחוֹר֙ מִלְכָּ֔ה בַּת־הָרָ֥ן אֲבִֽי־מִלְכָּ֖ה וַֽאֲבִ֥י יִסְכָּֽה׃

i18n.en: Abram and Nachor took for themselves wives. The name of Abram's wife was Sarai, and the name of Nachor's wife was Milkah, daughter of Haran, the father of Milkah and the father of Yiskah.
i18n.he: וַיִּקַּ֨ח אַבְרָ֧ם וְנָח֛וֹר לָהֶ֖ם נָשִׁ֑ים שֵׁ֤ם אֵֽשֶׁת־אַבְרָם֙ שָׂרָ֔י וְשֵׁ֤ם אֵֽשֶׁת־נָחוֹר֙ מִלְכָּ֔ה בַּת־הָרָ֥ן אֲבִֽי־מִלְכָּ֖ה וַֽאֲבִ֥י יִסְכָּֽה׃
i18n.de: Und Abram und Nachor nahmen sich Frauen. Der Name der Frau Abrams war Sarai, und der Name der Frau Nachors war Milka, die Tochter Harans, des Vaters Milkas und des Vaters Jiskas.
i18n.es: Abram y Najor tomaron para sí mujeres. El nombre de la mujer de Abram era Sarai, y el nombre de la mujer de Najor era Milcá, hija de Harán, padre de Milcá y padre de Iscá.
i18n.fr: Abram et Nahor prirent pour eux des femmes. Le nom de la femme d'Abram était Saraï, et le nom de la femme de Nahor était Milka, fille de Harân, le père de Milka et le père de Yiska.
i18n.ja: アブラムとナホルは妻を娶った。アブラムの妻の名はサライ。ナホルの妻の名はミルカで、ハランの娘である——ハランはミルカとイスカの父であった。
i18n.ko: 아브람과 나홀은 자기들을 위하여 아내들을 취하였다. 아브람의 아내의 이름은 사래였고, 나홀의 아내의 이름은 밀가였으니, 그녀는 하란의 딸이었고, 밀가의 아버지요 이스가의 아버지였다.
i18n.ru: И взяли Аврам и Нахор себе жён. Имя жены Аврама — Сарай, а имя жены Нахора — Милка, дочь Арана, отца Милки и отца Иски.
i18n.zh: 亚伯兰和拿鹤都娶了妻子。亚伯兰的妻子名叫撒莱，拿鹤的妻子名叫密迦，是哈兰的女儿——哈兰是密迦与亦迦的父亲。
i18n.zh-Hant: 亞伯蘭和拿鶴各自娶了妻子。亞伯蘭妻子的名叫撒萊，拿鶴妻子的名叫密迦—是哈蘭的女兒；哈蘭是密迦和亦迦的父親。

notes.official:
**The brides are named — and one is identified.** Sarai's lineage is not given; Milkah's is (she is Haran's daughter, niece to her husband Nachor — an intra-family marriage consistent with patriarchal-period norms). *Yiskah* is named only here in the Hebrew Bible; rabbinic tradition identifies her with Sarai (no textual evidence), or as a separate sister. The brevity is one of the chapter's textual cruces — the chapter leaves the relationship unresolved.

The naming of the wives anticipates Genesis 12+: Sarai will be central to the Abraham narrative; Milkah will be referenced again only as Rebekah's grandmother (24:15). The chapter is setting up the patriarchal family network through which the covenant will be transmitted.

paragraphs.text: וַתְּהִ֥י שָׂרַ֖י עֲקָרָ֑ה אֵ֥ין לָ֖הּ וָלָֽד׃

i18n.en: Sarai was barren — she had no child.
i18n.he: וַתְּהִ֥י שָׂרַ֖י עֲקָרָ֑ה אֵ֥ין לָ֖הּ וָלָֽד׃
i18n.de: Sarai aber war unfruchtbar — sie hatte kein Kind.
i18n.es: Sarai era estéril—no tenía hijo.
i18n.fr: Saraï était stérile — elle n'avait pas d'enfant.
i18n.ja: サライは不妊であった——彼女には子がなかった。
i18n.ko: 사래는 임신하지 못하였다 — 그녀에게는 아이가 없었다.
i18n.ru: А Сарай была бесплодна — не было у неё ребёнка.
i18n.zh: 撒莱不育——她没有孩子。
i18n.zh-Hant: 撒萊不能生育—她沒有孩子。

notes.official:
**The chapter's quiet pivot.** Six words in Hebrew set up the entire Abraham-Sarah cycle that will run through chapters 12–25. *Aqarah* — *barren* — names the condition that will be the load-bearing constraint of the next ten chapters: the covenant-line passes through a couple unable to produce children. The whole drama of the Abraham narrative — the divine promise of offspring, the years of waiting, the Hagar and Ishmael episode, the laughter of Sarah, the late birth of Isaac — turns on this single verse.

The redundant *ein lah valad* — *she had no child* — drives the point home: barrenness is the asserted fact, not just delayed conception. The chapter is foregrounding the obstacle the next narrative will overcome.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקַּ֨ח תֶּ֜רַח אֶת־אַבְרָ֣ם בְּנ֗וֹ וְאֶת־ל֤וֹט בֶּן־הָרָן֙ בֶּן־בְּנ֔וֹ וְאֵת֙ שָׂרַ֣י כַּלָּת֔וֹ אֵ֖שֶׁת אַבְרָ֣ם בְּנ֑וֹ וַיֵּצְא֨וּ אִתָּ֜ם מֵא֣וּר כַּשְׂדִּ֗ים לָלֶ֙כֶת֙ אַ֣רְצָה כְּנַ֔עַן וַיָּבֹ֥אוּ עַד־חָרָ֖ן וַיֵּ֥שְׁבוּ שָֽׁם׃

i18n.en: Terah took Abram his son, Lot the son of Haran his grandson, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, the wife of his son Abram; and they went out with them from Ur of the Kasdim to go to the land of Canaan, and they came to Haran and settled there.
i18n.he: וַיִּקַּ֨ח תֶּ֜רַח אֶת־אַבְרָ֣ם בְּנ֗וֹ וְאֶת־ל֤וֹט בֶּן־הָרָן֙ בֶּן־בְּנ֔וֹ וְאֵת֙ שָׂרַ֣י כַּלָּת֔וֹ אֵ֖שֶׁת אַבְרָ֣ם בְּנ֑וֹ וַיֵּצְא֨וּ אִתָּ֜ם מֵא֣וּר כַּשְׂדִּ֗ים לָלֶ֙כֶת֙ אַ֣רְצָה כְּנַ֔עַן וַיָּבֹ֥אוּ עַד־חָרָ֖ן וַיֵּ֥שְׁבוּ שָֽׁם׃
i18n.de: Und Terach nahm Abram, seinen Sohn, und Lot, den Sohn Harans, seinen Enkel, und Sarai, seine Schwiegertochter, die Frau seines Sohnes Abram; und sie zogen mit ihnen aus Ur der Kasdim aus, um in das Land Kanaan zu gehen, und sie kamen nach Haran und ließen sich dort nieder.
i18n.es: Téraj tomó a Abram su hijo, a Lot el hijo de Harán su nieto, y a Sarai su nuera, mujer de su hijo Abram; y salieron con ellos de Ur de los caldeos para ir a la tierra de Canaán, y llegaron hasta Harán y se establecieron allí.
i18n.fr: Térah prit Abram son fils, Lot le fils de Harân son petit-fils, et Saraï sa belle-fille, la femme de son fils Abram ; et ils sortirent avec eux d'Our des Chaldéens pour aller au pays de Kena'an, et ils vinrent à Harân et s'y établirent.
i18n.ja: テラはその子アブラム、その孫すなわちハランの子ロト、その嫁すなわち子アブラムの妻サライを連れて、カルデアのウルから共に出て、カナンの地へ行こうとした。彼らはハランに来て、そこに住みついた。
i18n.ko: 데라가 자기 아들 아브람, 자기 아들 하란의 아들인 자기 손자 롯, 그리고 자기 아들 아브람의 아내인 자기 며느리 사래를 데리고; 그들이 갈대아의 우르에서 그들과 함께 나와 가나안 땅으로 가려 하였으나, 하란에 이르러 거기에 정착하였다.
i18n.ru: И взял Терах Аврама, сына своего, и Лота, сына Арана, внука своего, и Сарай, невестку свою, жену Аврама, сына своего; и вышли они с ними из Ура Халдейского, чтобы идти в землю Ханаанскую, и пришли в Харан и поселились там.
i18n.zh: 他拉带着他的儿子亚伯兰，并他孙子哈兰的儿子罗得，与他的儿妇——他儿子亚伯兰的妻子撒莱——一同出了迦勒底的吾珥，要往迦南地去；他们到了哈兰，就住在那里。
i18n.zh-Hant: 他拉帶著他的兒子亞伯蘭、他的孫子—哈蘭的兒子羅得，以及他的兒婦—就是他兒子亞伯蘭的妻子撒萊，與他們一同從迦勒底的吾珥出來，要往迦南地去；他們來到哈蘭就住在那裡。

notes.official:
**The unfinished journey.** Terah, not Abram, is the verse's grammatical subject — *vayyiqach Terah* (Terah took). The family's exit from Ur is at Terah's initiative; Abram is the *passenger* of his father's migration. The destination is *artzah Kena'an* — *toward the land of Canaan* — the same Canaan whose boundaries chapter 10:19 sketched in anticipation.

But they do not arrive. *Vayavo'u ad-Charan vayyeshvu sham* — *they came as far as Haran and settled there*. Haran (חָרָן) is a major northern Mesopotamian city (the site near modern Harran in southeastern Turkey), an important Bronze and Iron Age trading center on the Aramaean / Mesopotamian frontier. The family stops short of Canaan; Terah will die in Haran (v32). The migration toward Canaan is interrupted.

Chapter 12 will open with YHWH's call to Abram to *go from your land, from your kindred, from your father's house, to the land that I will show you* (12:1) — and Abram will *complete* the migration his father had begun and abandoned. The Wheel of Heaven lens reads the seam: the journey toward Canaan begins under Terah's initiative without divine prompting, stalls at Haran, and resumes under explicit divine call. The covenant-line is positioned as completing what the family-line could not.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּהְי֣וּ יְמֵי־תֶ֔רַח חָמֵ֥שׁ שָׁנִ֖ים וּמָאתַ֣יִם שָׁנָ֑ה וַיָּ֥מָת תֶּ֖רַח בְּחָרָֽן׃ (ס)

i18n.en: The days of Terah were two hundred and five years, and Terah died in Haran.
i18n.he: וַיִּהְי֣וּ יְמֵי־תֶ֔רַח חָמֵ֥שׁ שָׁנִ֖ים וּמָאתַ֣יִם שָׁנָ֑ה וַיָּ֥מָת תֶּ֖רַח בְּחָרָֽן׃ (ס)
i18n.de: Und die Tage Terachs waren zweihundertfünf Jahre, und Terach starb in Haran.
i18n.es: Y los días de Téraj fueron doscientos cinco años, y Téraj murió en Harán.
i18n.fr: Les jours de Térah furent deux cent cinq ans, et Térah mourut à Harân.
i18n.ja: テラの日々は二百五年であった。そしてテラはハランで死んだ。
i18n.ko: 데라의 날은 이백오 년이었고, 데라는 하란에서 죽었다.
i18n.ru: И было дней Тераха двести пять лет, и умер Терах в Харане.
i18n.zh: 他拉一生的日子共二百零五年；他拉就死在哈兰。
i18n.zh-Hant: 他拉共活了二百零五年，他拉死在哈蘭。

notes.official:
**The primaeval-history arc closes.** Terah's 205-year lifespan is the chapter's closing data-point; his death in Haran is the chapter's closing event. The primaeval-history block of Genesis 1–11 ends here — at a death, in a transitional city, with a stalled migration. The next chapter opens with the divine call that will turn the family's incomplete journey into the foundational journey of the patriarchal narrative.

The transition from primaeval history to patriarchal narrative is structurally clean: Genesis 1–11 has moved from cosmos (ch 1) to humanity (chs 2–3) to family (chs 4–5) to the cosmic reset (chs 6–9) to the ethnographic catalogue (ch 10) to the Babel cap (ch 11:1–9) to the genealogy (11:10–26) to the household-narrative threshold (11:27–32). Each successive section narrows the scope. Chapter 12 will narrow further: from Terah's whole household to a single called man — Abram — and a single destination — the land YHWH will show him.
